source.text: Despite Martin Luther's harsh polemics against his Roman Catholic opponents over issues concerning Mary and the saints, theologians appear to agree that Luther adhered to the Marian decrees of the ecumenical councils and dogmas of the church. He held fast to the belief that Mary was a perpetual virgin and the Theotokos or Mother of God. Special attention is given to the assertion that Luther, some three-hundred years before the dogmatization of the Immaculate Conception by Pope Pius IX in 1854, was a firm adherent of that view. Others maintain that Luther in later years changed his position on the Immaculate Conception, which, at that time was undefined in the Church, maintaining however the sinlessness of Mary throughout her life. For Luther, early in his life, the Assumption of Mary was an understood fact, although he later stated that the Bible did not say anything about it and stopped celebrating its feast. Important to him was the belief that Mary and the saints do live on after death. "Throughout his career as a priest-professor-reformer, Luther preached, taught, and argued about the veneration of Mary with a verbosity that ranged from childlike piety to sophisticated polemics. His views are intimately linked to his Christocentric theology and its consequences for liturgy and piety." Luther, while revering Mary, came to criticize the "Papists" for blurring the line, between high admiration of the grace of God wherever it is seen in a human being, and religious service given to another creature. He considered the Roman Catholic practice of celebrating saints' days and making intercessory requests addressed especially to Mary and other departed saints to be idolatry. His final thoughts on Marian devotion and veneration are preserved in a sermon preached at Wittenberg only a month before his death:
source.title: Mary, mother of Jesus

source.text: Although there had been significant earlier attempts to reform the Catholic Church before Luther -- such as those of Jan Hus, Peter Waldo, and John Wycliffe -- Martin Luther is widely acknowledged to have started the Reformation with the Ninety - five Theses. Luther began by criticising the sale of indulgences, insisting that the Pope had no authority over purgatory and that the Catholic doctrine of the merits of the saints had no foundation in the Bible. The Protestant Reformation, however, would come to incorporate doctrinal changes such as a complete reliance on Scripture as a source of proper belief (sola scriptura) and the belief that faith in Jesus, and not good works, is the only way to obtain God's pardon for sin (sola fide). The core motivation behind these changes was theological, though many other factors played a part, including the rise of nationalism, the Western Schism that eroded loyalty to the Papacy, the perceived corruption of the Roman Curia, the impact of humanism, and the new learning of the Renaissance that questioned much traditional thought.
source.title: Reformation

EXPERIMENT TASK — WRITE SPARQL FOR MUSIQUE QUESTION

Prompt version: musique-sparql-evidence-first-v1

ROLE

You are constructing the SPARQL computation for a multi-hop question-answering
experiment over a frozen RDF graph.

Your job is not merely to state or force the expected answer.

Your job is to express a query whose ?answer value is obtained by executing
graph patterns against the RDF graph supplied below.

WHY THE QUERY STRUCTURE MATTERS

The query is executed over the frozen graph.

After execution, the computation is traced backwards to determine which RDF
statements contributed to each returned answer, and those RDF statements are
resolved back to their exact source occurrences.

Therefore the answer must genuinely arise from graph matching.

A query that simply injects an already-known answer may return the right value,
but it does not express the computation we need to observe.

THE FROZEN GRAPH IS THE SOURCE OF TRUTH FOR THIS TASK

Every triple pattern you rely on must correspond to relations actually available
in the frozen RDF graph.

Do not invent a relation because it would make the reasoning chain work.

Do not assume a benchmark relation exists unless you can locate the corresponding
RDF triple in the supplied graph.

If the graph does not contain the relation needed for an intended reasoning
step, do not fabricate it.

DECOMPOSITION

The MuSiQue decomposition describes the intended semantic dependency of the
question.

Use it to understand what each reasoning step means and to look for corresponding
relations in the frozen graph.

The decomposition does not create facts in the graph.

An intermediate answer from the decomposition may help you recognize entities,
but the SPARQL computation must still derive its bindings through the graph
relations that actually exist.

CONSTRUCT THE QUERY

Find the RDF triples in the frozen graph that can realize the question.

Use variables to connect dependent graph patterns.

The final ?answer variable must occur in an RDF triple pattern that retrieves
its value from the graph.

Example:

Graph:
    <Organization> <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .

To retrieve the organization represented by FIFA:

    ?answer <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .

Do not instead write:

    <Organization> <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .
    BIND(<Organization> AS ?answer)

The first query derives the answer.
The second query inserts an answer that was already known.

SUPPORTED QUERY FORM

Use a SELECT query with ?answer as the answer variable.

Use basic RDF triple patterns and joins through shared variables.

Do not use:
- BIND
- VALUES
- SELECT DISTINCT
- GRAPH
- SERVICE
- SPARQL updates
- FROM clauses

Python adds dataset scoping after your semantic query is produced.

MATCHED TRIPLES

matched_triples is your record of the exact frozen-graph statements you relied
on while constructing the query.

Copy those N-Triples lines exactly from the supplied frozen graph.

Do not report a triple that is not present in the graph.

matched_triples describes your evidence selection; the SPARQL query describes
the computation you construct from that evidence.

OUTPUT

Return only valid JSON:

{
  "matched_triples": [
    "<subject> <predicate> <object> ."
  ],
  "sparql": "SELECT ?answer WHERE { ... }"
}

source.text: Despite Martin Luther's harsh polemics against his Roman Catholic opponents over issues concerning Mary and the saints, theologians appear to agree that Luther adhered to the Marian decrees of the ecumenical councils and dogmas of the church. He held fast to the belief that Mary was a perpetual virgin and the Theotokos or Mother of God. Special attention is given to the assertion that Luther, some three-hundred years before the dogmatization of the Immaculate Conception by Pope Pius IX in 1854, was a firm adherent of that view. Others maintain that Luther in later years changed his position on the Immaculate Conception, which, at that time was undefined in the Church, maintaining however the sinlessness of Mary throughout her life. For Luther, early in his life, the Assumption of Mary was an understood fact, although he later stated that the Bible did not say anything about it and stopped celebrating its feast. Important to him was the belief that Mary and the saints do live on after death. "Throughout his career as a priest-professor-reformer, Luther preached, taught, and argued about the veneration of Mary with a verbosity that ranged from childlike piety to sophisticated polemics. His views are intimately linked to his Christocentric theology and its consequences for liturgy and piety." Luther, while revering Mary, came to criticize the "Papists" for blurring the line, between high admiration of the grace of God wherever it is seen in a human being, and religious service given to another creature. He considered the Roman Catholic practice of celebrating saints' days and making intercessory requests addressed especially to Mary and other departed saints to be idolatry. His final thoughts on Marian devotion and veneration are preserved in a sermon preached at Wittenberg only a month before his death:
source.title: Mary, mother of Jesus

source.text: Although there had been significant earlier attempts to reform the Catholic Church before Luther -- such as those of Jan Hus, Peter Waldo, and John Wycliffe -- Martin Luther is widely acknowledged to have started the Reformation with the Ninety - five Theses. Luther began by criticising the sale of indulgences, insisting that the Pope had no authority over purgatory and that the Catholic doctrine of the merits of the saints had no foundation in the Bible. The Protestant Reformation, however, would come to incorporate doctrinal changes such as a complete reliance on Scripture as a source of proper belief (sola scriptura) and the belief that faith in Jesus, and not good works, is the only way to obtain God's pardon for sin (sola fide). The core motivation behind these changes was theological, though many other factors played a part, including the rise of nationalism, the Western Schism that eroded loyalty to the Papacy, the perceived corruption of the Roman Curia, the impact of humanism, and the new learning of the Renaissance that questioned much traditional thought.
source.title: Reformation
